It differs from [Quaternion to SO3 Conversion](2305-quaternion-to-so3-conversion.md) by operating directly on vectors rather than converting the rotation representation to a matrix format [S3474-quaternion-operations.md].
- Quaternion $q$: Stored as a 4-element structure or array.
- **Non-unit Quaternion**: If $q$ is not normalized, the result will be scaled incorrectly.
- **Precision**: For very small rotations or near-zero vectors, standard floating-point arithmetic may introduce minor errors.
- **Input Format**: Ensure the quaternion convention (scalar-first vs. vector-first) matches the implementation.
**Strengths:** No gimbal lock; computationally efficient for single rotations; smooth interpolation capabilities (SLERP) are inherent to the representation [S3474-quaternion-operations.md].

**Limitations:** Requires normalization to maintain unit length; less intuitive for visualizing rotations compared to matrices; composing multiple rotations requires quaternion multiplication, not addition [S3474-quaternion-operations.md].
**When to use:** When rotating individual vectors (e.g., normals, rays, points) by a known quaternion orientation.

**When not to use:** When transforming entire coordinate systems or when matrix operations are already dominant in the pipeline (in which case [Rotation Matrix Computation](2280-rotation-matrix-computation.md) might be more cache-friendly for batched operations).
Quaternion rotation was introduced by William Rowan Hamilton in 1843 [unofficial].

In computer graphics and volume rendering, it has become a standard method for representing 3D orientations due to its compactness (4 numbers vs 9 for a matrix) and numerical stability [S3474-quaternion-operations.md].
